imo-1974-01.title: Find the number of rounds and the cards
imo-1974-01.body:
Let $n\ge 2$ be the number of rounds. In every round exactly $p+q+r$ counters are handed out, so
$$n(p+q+r)=20+10+9=39 .$$
Since $p\ge1,\ q\ge2,\ r\ge3$, we have $p+q+r\ge 6$, so $p+q+r$ is a divisor of $39=3\cdot13$ that is at least $6$, i.e. $13$ or $39$. As $n\ge2$, we get $p+q+r=13$ and $n=3$.

**Bounds on $r$.** $A$ received $20$ counters in three rounds, each time at most $r$, so $3r\ge 20$ and $r\ge 7$. $B$ received $r$ in the last round and at least $p\ge1$ in each of the other two rounds, so $r+2\le r+2p\le 10$, i.e. $r\le 8$.

* If $r=7$: then $p+q=6$ with $p\ge1$, so $q\le5$. $A$'s three cards total $21$ if all are $7$, and otherwise at most $7+7+5=19$; so $A$ cannot have $20$. Impossible.
* So $r=8$ and $p+q=5$. $B$ got $8$ in the last round and $2$ in the other two rounds together, each at least $p$; hence $p=1$ (both times), and $q=4$.

**Who got what.** Each card is dealt once per round, so in total each card is dealt $3$ times. $B$ got $8,1,1$ (with the $8$ last). $A$ needs $20$ from three of the values $1,4,8$: the only way is $8+8+4$. Then $C$ got the remaining cards: $4,4,1$ (total $9$, as required).

In the last round $B$ had $r=8$, so in the first round $B$ had $p=1$. $A$ had $q=4$ in only one round; the card $r$ was given to $A$ in the two rounds in which $B$ did not have it, which include the first round. So in the first round $A$ had $r$, $B$ had $p$, and therefore $C$ had $q$.

**Answer: $C$** (and the cards were $p=1$, $q=4$, $r=8$, played for $3$ rounds). ∎

imo-1974-02.title: Power of a point and the height of an arc
imo-1974-02.body:
Let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$ (centre $O$, radius $R$), let $h_c$ be the distance from $C$ to line $AB$, and let $\mathcal A$ be the arc $AB$ of $\Gamma$ not containing $C$.

**Step 1: reformulation.** Let $D$ be a point of side $AB$; clearly $D\ne A,B$ is needed (at $D=A$ we would need $CA^2=0$). Let line $CD$ meet $\Gamma$ again at $E$; $E$ lies on $\mathcal A$ (the chord $CE$ crosses chord $AB$ at the interior point $D$). By the power of the point $D$,
$$AD\cdot DB = CD\cdot DE .$$
Hence $CD^2 = AD\cdot DB \iff CD = DE \iff D$ is the midpoint of $CE$. Since $C$ and $E$ lie on opposite sides of $AB$, the midpoint of $CE$ lies on line $AB$ exactly when $E$ and $C$ have the same distance from line $AB$.

So: *such a $D$ exists iff some point $E\in\mathcal A$ has distance exactly $h_c$ from line $AB$.* Indeed, if $D$ exists, the point $E$ above works. Conversely, if $E\in\mathcal A$ has distance $h_c$ from $AB$, the midpoint $D$ of $CE$ lies on line $AB$; it also lies inside the disc (on the chord $CE$), so it lies on the chord $AB$, i.e. on side $AB$; and $E$ is the second intersection of $CD$ with $\Gamma$, so $CD=DE$ gives $CD^2=AD\cdot DB$.

**Step 2: the distances from $AB$ of points of $\mathcal A$.** The distance to line $AB$ is a continuous function on the arc $\mathcal A$, equal to $0$ at $A$ and $B$ and largest at the midpoint $T$ of the arc (the point of $\mathcal A$ on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, farthest from the chord). By the intermediate value theorem it takes exactly the values in $[0, d(T)]$. The arc $\mathcal A$ has central angle $2C$ (inscribed angle theorem), so $O$ is at signed distance $R\cos C$ from $AB$ on the side of $C$ and
$$d(T)=R-R\cos C = 2R\sin^2\tfrac C2$$
(this also holds when $C\ge 90^\circ$, where $\cos C\le 0$).

**Step 3: compute $h_c$.** $h_c = a\sin B = 2R\sin A\sin B$ by the law of sines.

So $D$ exists $\iff h_c\le d(T) \iff 2R\sin A\sin B\le 2R\sin^2\frac C2 \iff \sin A\sin B\le\sin^2\frac C2$. ∎

imo-1974-03.title: Conjugates in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 8]$
imo-1974-03.body:
By the binomial theorem,
$$(1+\sqrt8)^{2n+1}=\sum_{j=0}^{2n+1}\binom{2n+1}{j}(\sqrt8)^j = a+b\sqrt8,$$
where the even terms $j=2k$ give $a=\sum_k\binom{2n+1}{2k}8^k$ and the odd terms $j=2k+1$ give $b\sqrt8$ with
$$b=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{2n+1}{2k+1}8^k=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{2n+1}{2k+1}2^{3k},$$
which is exactly our number. Both $a,b$ are integers, and the same computation with $-\sqrt8$ gives $(1-\sqrt8)^{2n+1}=a-b\sqrt8$. Multiplying,
$$a^2-8b^2=\big((1+\sqrt8)(1-\sqrt8)\big)^{2n+1}=(-7)^{2n+1}=-7^{2n+1}.$$
Suppose $5\mid b$. Then modulo $5$:
$$a^2\equiv -7^{2n+1} = -7\cdot 49^n\equiv -2\cdot(-1)^n \equiv \pm 2 \pmod 5 .$$
But squares modulo $5$ are only $0,1,4$, and $\pm2\equiv 2,3$. Contradiction. Hence $5\nmid b$ for every $n\ge0$. ∎

imo-1974-04.title: Count, exclude one case, construct the rest
imo-1974-04.body:
The rectangles are made of whole squares of the board (the decomposition is along grid lines). The $i$-th rectangle has $a_i$ white and $a_i$ black squares, so its area is $2a_i$, and the areas add up to $64$:
$$a_1+a_2+\cdots+a_p=32 .$$

**Upper bound.** The $a_i$ are distinct positive integers, so $a_1+\cdots+a_p\ge 1+2+\cdots+p=\frac{p(p+1)}2$. For $p=8$ this is $36>32$, so $p\le 7$.

**Candidates for $p=7$.** We need $7$ distinct positive integers with sum $32$, i.e. $4$ more than $1+2+\cdots+7=28$. Writing $a_i=i+d_i$ with $0\le d_1\le d_2\le\cdots\le d_7$ (the $a_i$ strictly increase iff $d_i$ is non-decreasing) and $\sum d_i=4$, the $d$'s correspond to partitions of $4$:
* $4$: $(1,2,3,4,5,6,11)$;
* $3+1$: $(1,2,3,4,5,7,10)$;
* $2+2$: $(1,2,3,4,6,7,9)$;
* $2+1+1$: $(1,2,3,4,5,8,9)$;
* $1+1+1+1$: $(1,2,3,5,6,7,8)$.

The first is impossible: $a_7=11$ needs a rectangle of area $22=1\cdot22=2\cdot11$, which does not fit in an $8\times8$ board.

**Constructions.** Any rectangle of even area on a chessboard has one side of even length, so it splits into dominoes and has equal numbers of white and black squares; so condition (i) holds automatically for rectangles of area $2a_i$. Here are tilings for the other four sequences (each cell shows the $a_i$ of its rectangle):
```
(1,2,3,4,5,7,10)          (1,2,3,4,5,8,9)
 1  1  2  2  2  2  3  3    1  1  2  2  2  2  3  3
 4  4  4  4  7  7  3  3    4  4  8  8  8  8  3  3
 4  4  4  4  7  7  3  3    4  4  8  8  8  8  3  3
10 10 10 10  7  7  5  5    4  4  8  8  8  8  5  5
10 10 10 10  7  7  5  5    4  4  8  8  8  8  5  5
10 10 10 10  7  7  5  5    9  9  9  9  9  9  5  5
10 10 10 10  7  7  5  5    9  9  9  9  9  9  5  5
10 10 10 10  7  7  5  5    9  9  9  9  9  9  5  5

(1,2,3,4,6,7,9)           (1,2,3,5,6,7,8)
 1  1  2  2  2  2  3  3    1  1  2  2  2  2  3  3
 7  7  4  4  4  4  3  3    6  6  6  6  7  7  3  3
 7  7  4  4  4  4  3  3    6  6  6  6  7  7  3  3
 7  7  6  6  6  6  6  6    6  6  6  6  7  7  5  5
 7  7  6  6  6  6  6  6    8  8  8  8  7  7  5  5
 7  7  9  9  9  9  9  9    8  8  8  8  7  7  5  5
 7  7  9  9  9  9  9  9    8  8  8  8  7  7  5  5
 7  7  9  9  9  9  9  9    8  8  8  8  7  7  5  5
```

**Answer: $p_{\max}=7$**, with $(a_1,\ldots,a_7)$ equal to $(1,2,3,4,5,7,10)$, $(1,2,3,4,5,8,9)$, $(1,2,3,4,6,7,9)$ or $(1,2,3,5,6,7,8)$. ∎

imo-1974-05.title: Bounds plus continuity
imo-1974-05.body:
**$S>1$.** Each denominator is smaller than $a+b+c+d$, so
$$S>\frac{a+b+c+d}{a+b+c+d}=1 .$$

**$S<2$.** Use $\frac{x}{y+z}<\frac{x}{y}$ type estimates, pairing $a$ with $b$ and $c$ with $d$:
$$\frac{a}{a+b+d}<\frac{a}{a+b},\quad \frac{b}{a+b+c}<\frac{b}{a+b},\quad \frac{c}{b+c+d}<\frac{c}{c+d},\quad\frac{d}{a+c+d}<\frac{d}{c+d},$$
so $S<1+1=2$.

**Every value in $(1,2)$ occurs.** For $t>0$:
* $(a,b,c,d)=(1,1,t,t)$ gives $S_1(t)=\dfrac{2}{2+t}+\dfrac{2t}{1+2t}$;
* $(a,b,c,d)=(1,t,1,t)$ gives $S_2(t)=\dfrac{2}{1+2t}+\dfrac{2t}{2+t}$.

Both are continuous on $(0,1]$, with $S_1(1)=S_2(1)=\frac43$, $S_1(t)\to1$ and $S_2(t)\to2$ as $t\to0^+$. By the intermediate value theorem $S_1$ takes every value in $(1,\frac43]$ and $S_2$ every value in $[\frac43,2)$.

**Answer: the set of values of $S$ is the open interval $(1,2)$.** ∎

imo-1974-06.title: Divisibility $u-v\mid P(u)-P(v)$
imo-1974-06.body:
Let $d=\deg P\ge1$, let $U$ be the set of integer roots of $P(x)=1$ and $V$ the set of integer roots of $P(x)=-1$, so $n(P)=|U|+|V|$ and $|U|,|V|\le d$ (a non-constant polynomial of degree $d$ takes each value at most $d$ times).

**If $U$ or $V$ is empty**, then $n(P)\le d$ and we are done. So assume both are non-empty.

**Key lemma: $|U|\le3$ and $|V|\le3$.** Let $U=\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}$. Since $P-1$ has integer coefficients and vanishes at the $u_i$, we can divide by the monic factors: $P(x)-1=(x-u_1)\cdots(x-u_k)Q(x)$ with $Q\in\mathbb Z[x]$. Take any $v\in V$:
$$-2=P(v)-1=(v-u_1)(v-u_2)\cdots(v-u_k)\,Q(v).$$
So the $k$ *distinct* nonzero integers $v-u_i$ have a product dividing $2$. Each has absolute value $1$ or $2$; at most one has absolute value $2$ (otherwise $4$ divides the product), and at most two have absolute value $1$ (namely $1$ and $-1$). So $k\le 3$. By symmetry ($-P$ swaps $U$ and $V$), $|V|\le3$.

**Case $d\ge4$:** $n(P)\le 3+3=6\le d+2$.

**Case $d\le 2$:** $n(P)\le 2d\le d+2$.

**Case $d=3$:** we must exclude $n(P)=6$, i.e. $|U|=|V|=3$. Then $P(x)-1=c(x-u_1)(x-u_2)(x-u_3)$ with $c\in\mathbb Z$, and for each $v\in V$ the three distinct numbers $v-u_i$ have product dividing $2$; by the lemma's argument they are $1,-1$ and $\pm2$. Thus $v-1,v+1\in U$ and the third element of $U$ is $v\pm2$; in either case $v$ is the unique integer strictly between $\min U$ and $\max U$ that is not in $U$ (for $U=\{v-1,v+1,v+2\}$ or $U=\{v-2,v-1,v+1\}$). So $v$ is determined by $U$, giving $|V|\le1$, a contradiction. Hence $n(P)\le5=d+2$.

In all cases $n(P)-\deg P\le 2$. ∎
